Next, the corresponding opal dye (opal 480 FP150001KT, opal 520 FP1487001KT, opal 570 FP1488001KT, opal 620 FP1495001KT, opal 690 FP1497001KT and opal 780 FP1501001KT, Akoya Biosciences) were applied, previously prepared following the manufacturer’s instructions. After each application of the primary antibody, followed by the corresponding secondary antibody and opal dye (with increasing fluorophore excitation wavelength), an antibody neutralization and denaturation step was applied to remove residual antibodies and HRP, before starting the staining cycle again with the Discovery inhibitor blocking step. Finally, samples were counterstained with DAPI (Roche). When used, fluorescein-labelled Jacalin (FL-1151-5, Vector Laboratories) was integrated into the mIF staining protocol by swapping it with the 520 opal dye and always applied last in the staining protocol.

According to recent reports, as previously described52, opal mIF stainings were imaged and digitized using multispectral imaging of the Vectra Polaris (Perkin Elmer) using the MOTiF technology at ×20 magnification for all seven opal dyes (opal 480–780) and DAPI. Slides were imaged in a batch manner to ensure identical imaging settings and cross-comparability within each experiment for subsequent image analysis. Unmixing of channels and processing of images were performed with PhenoChart (v1.0.12) and inForm (v2.4). Images were processed as .qptiff tiles and fused in HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs). A pixel resolution of 0.5 µm per pixel was used.

High-resolution opal mIF images were obtained using a STELLARIS 8 microscope (Leica) with a water-immersion objective (HC FLUOTAR L VISIR ×25/0.95 NA WATER). A white-light laser (440–790 nm) was used to image all opal dyes. Channel signals were acquired sequentially to reduce cross-bleeding. Images were obtained in bidirectional mode with 1,024 × 1,024 pixels (pixel size of 384.56 × 384.56 nm2) or 2,048 × 2,048 pixels (pixel size of 273.8 × 273.38 nm2). Images were either visualized as maximum projection or 3D reconstructed using the Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) software (v4.6.1.27508).

Image analysis of opal mIF images was performed with HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs) and HALO AI (v3.6.4134, Indica Labs). Sample annotation was either manually performed or by deploying the TMA module in HALO. For detection and annotation of the engineered intestines, a RandomForest (v2) classifier was used to distinguish organoids from background (for example, matrix; minimum object size more than 1,000 µm). Following validation, engineered intestines were handled as individual regions of interest (ROIs) and quantification was executed per ROI. The RandomForest (v2) classifier was integrated in the Area Quantification FL (v2.3.4) modules and used to quantify positive marker staining against either overall size of each individual object or normalized to the DAPI+ area of the object (as indicated in the figure legends) as well as for quantification of intensities. The HighPlex FL (v4.2.14) module was used to perform nuclear segmentation based on DAPI+ cells, assisted by HALO AI’s integrated ‘AI default nuclear segmentation type’) for phenotype analysis. The FISH-IF (v2.2.5) module was used to perform DAPI-based nuclear segmentation and identification of cells positive for single intracellular bacteria. Specific cell phenotypes were determined by colocalization of the respective markers of interest with the DAPI+ nuclei (including the cytoplasm radius (1.25 µm) and nuclear signals, depending on the marker of interest). By integrating the RandomForest (v2) or DenseNet (v2) classifier in the HighPlex analysis module, for example, localization of the T cells in the matrix or epithelium, was determined.

Sources indicate that assessment of the spatial patterning was performed by manually annotating the crypts and the top epithelial layer along the E-cadherin+ signal as separate ROIs. The basal side of the top epithelial layer served as the ROI border to the crypt underneath. Cell quantification was then performed within the separate annotations per engineered intestine using the Highplex FL module. Similarly, quantification of the thickness of mucus was performed by manually outlining two lines within the same annotation layer: one along the apical side of the E-cadherin+ epithelium of the top epithelial layer (excluding the crypt depth), and a second line along the lumen-facing top layer of the Jacalin+ mucus.

In a recent development, positive controls on primary matched or non-matched primary intestinal tissue were included in every staining. In case of some experiments, negative controls were co-embedded within the same histoarray by experimental design, easing unbiased threshold adjustment and detection of potential unspecific antibody binding (for example, the epithelium-only control served as the negative control for immune markers; different intestinal regions within one FFPE block).

Industry observers note that quantification of the number of viable crypts per engineered intestine was performed with a RandomForest classifier (v2) in HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs). Dozens of viable intestinal crypts from different donors were manually annotated using brightfield images of the engineered intestines acquired with the ×2 objective of the Leica Dmi1 inverted microscope (11526227, Leica Microsystems). After brief verification, the algorithm was deployed to detect the number of viable crypts per engineered intestine. All brightfield images were acquired with the Leica Dmi1 inverted microscope with ×2, ×4 and ×10 objectives.

Statistical analysis was carried out with GraphPad Prism (v10.6.1; GraphPad software). The number of donors is indicated as ‘d = x’, whereas the number of independent engineered intestines within each donor is referred to as ‘n = x’ in the respective figure legend. The number of repeated independent experiments is indicated as ‘e = x’. Data normality was evaluated with Shapiro–Wilk normality test and Q–Q plots. When comparing two sets of data, paired or unpaired two-tailed t-tests were carried out, including Welch’s correction when the standard deviation determined not identical between the groups by a F-test. In case the data were not normally distributed, Mann–Whitney sum-rank tests were performed. For comparisons involving more than two datasets and multiple variables, we performed one-way and two-way ANOVA, including Tukey’s, Dunnett’s or Šídák’s multiple comparisons test comparisons when comparing to a control condition. Nested one-way ANOVA was performed when d < 3, comparing the data across the number of independent engineered intestines (n). A Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparison test was performed instead of one-way ANOVA when the data did not follow normal distribution. Data were visualized with their mean and standard deviation, with the exact P values highlighting the statistical significance in the respective figure legend.

Before dissociation, surfaces were cleaned with RNase AWAY Decontamination Reagent (10328011, Invitrogen) and all tubes were coated with a coating solution containing HBSS −Ca2+/−Mg2+ (14175095, Gibco) + 1% BSA (130-091-376, Miltenyi Biotec) at 4 °C for at least 15 min. Multiple engineered intestines were pooled for each scRNA-seq and scMultiome, as indicated in the figure legends. Intestinal monolayers were detached from the matrix, collected and transferred to DNA LoBind 1.5-ml tubes (22431021, Eppendorf) with 1 ml of coating solution using forceps. In the case of the scMultiome experiment, where the epithelium integrity was compromised, the epithelium and hydrogel matrix were apically punched using a 3-mm puncher and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube. The punched hydrogel was dissolved by incubating the mix with 1 ml of collagenase type I (100 U ml−1; 17100017, Gibco) in Advanced DMEM/F12 for 15 min at 37 °C, following three washing steps in coating solution to clean the presence of collagenase in the sample and remove the digested hydrogel. Pooled and cleaned monolayers were pipetted up and down 50 times to mechanically disrupt the monolayers into smaller fragments. The single-cell dissociation was performed using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (130-092-628, Miltenyi Biotec). In brief, the samples were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was removed and the samples were incubated with 1 ml of the enzymeP Mix 1 at 37 °C for a total of 15 min, homogenizing the sample every 5 min by pipetting up and down a total of 50 times with a P1000 tip. After the first incubation, 30 µl of enzyme A Mix2 was added to the sample and incubated for 10 min, with homogenization steps every 5 min and inspection of the suspension under a brightfield microscope. The single-cell suspension was filtered through a PluriStrainer Mini 40 µm (43-10040-40, Pluriselect), previously coated with coating solution, into newly introduced 1.5-ml DNA LoBind tubes and centrifuged at 450g for 5 min at 4 °C.

Industry observers note that for scRNA-seq or scMultiome experiments, the pellets were washed a total of three times with coating solution at 450g for 5 min at 4 °C. Next, the samples were counted using the Countless 3 FL (AMQAF2000, Invitrogen) and adjusted to the desired concentrations for multiplexing, nuclei isolation or loading on the Chromium X (10X Genomics).

For flow cytometry, FACS and Imagestream experiments, the pellets were washed 1× in DPBS before incubation with eBioscience Fixable Viability Dye eFluor 780 (1:2,000; 65-0865-14, Thermo Scientific) + TruStain FcX (1:200; 422301, BioLegend) in DPBS for 5 min at 4 °C in dark conditions. Next, the samples were spinned down, resuspended in FACS buffer (DPBS supplemented with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS), and incubated with PE-EpCAM (1:100; 324206, BioLegend) for 5 min at 4 °C in dark conditions. Single stained and unstained controls were prepared in parallel for compensation. After FACS, the sorted cells were centrifuged, resuspended in FACS buffer and counted before loading on the Chromium X.

Cell suspensions were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C before filtering through 70-µm strainers. For flow cytometric quantification of S.TmGFP-infected cells, fully stained, single stained and unstained samples were resuspended in 250 µl of FACS buffer and analysed using a five-laser Cytek Aurora spectral flow cytometer. Spectral unmixing with autofluorescence extraction was performed using Cytek Spectroflo CS software, and quantification of GFP+ cell fractions was performed in FlowJo (v10; BD Biosciences).

For FACS, fully stained, single stained and unstained samples were resuspended in 150 µl of FACS buffer. Bulk GFP+ and GFP− populations were isolated using a five-laser Cytek Aurora CS spectral cell sorter equipped with a 100-µm nozzle. Spectral unmixing with autofluorescence extraction was performed using Cytek Spectroflo CS software. Target cell populations were collected into low protein-binding 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes (Eppendorf). Next, the cells were centrifuged, resuspended in FACS buffer and counted for scRNA-seq on the Chromium X.

Sources indicate that for single-cell total RNA-seq (VASA-seq), single cells were index sorted using a five-laser BD FACSAria Fusion with a 100-µm nozzle into individual wells of a 384-well plate filled with lysis buffer (Single Cell Discoveries). Cells were grouped and sorted by GFP level (GFP−, GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi) to ensure equal representation in the final dataset of each group. Following sorting, plates were immediately stored at −80 °C until library preparation. Additional cells were also sorted into a lysis buffer containing 0.5% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich) for CFU counting within the same experiment.

Industry observers note that sorted GFP+ and GFP− cells were concentrated by centrifugation and resuspended in 25 µl of FACS buffer for analysis using a four-laser Cytek Amnis ImagestremX MKII dual CCD camera imaging flow cytometer. The 488-nm and 642-nm excitation lasers were set to a power of 10 mW and 150 mW, respectively, and data were acquired using the ×60 objective. Brightfield images were collected in channels 1 and 9, whereas fluorescence signals for GFP, EpCAM-PE and eFluor-780 were detected in channels 2, 3 and 12, respectively.

It has been revealed that imageStream data were analysed using IDEAS (v6.4.9.0). For each dataset, a compensation matrix was generated using the single-colour controls and the software compensation wizard, and applied to the relevant dataset. Events were gated to only keep contrasted, unclipped, EpCAM+GFP+ images of single host cells. The IDEAS internalization tool (GFP) was used to filter for host cells displaying intracellular GFP signal from the analysis and to quantify the prevalence of bacterial internalization. To perform spot counting in host cells, another filtering step to discard unfocused GFP signal was performed. With this filtering in place, we could start performing GFP spot counting using a series of machine learning classifiers. This was performed using IDEAS machine learning functionality. First, we manually selected two mutually exclusive populations of cells: 25 cells displaying a single GFP colony, 25 cells showing 2 or more than 2 colonies. A first machine learning classifier was trained on these two populations, and subsequently used to classify cells in two categories: ‘one colony’ and ‘more than one colony’. From the more-than-one-colony pool of events, the same strategy was used to train a second machine learning model on two mutually exclusive populations: 25 cells displaying 2 colonies, and 25 cells displaying more than 2 colonies. The model was run on the more than one colony data to classify cells in two new categories: two colonies versus more than two colonies. The obtained mutually exclusive populations were manually curated to fix misclassification of a few events. Cells belonging to the more-than-two-colonies population were manually classified into further populations: ‘three colonies’ and ‘more than three colonies’. Of note, the features weighting the most in our two machine learning classifiers were related to the area and ellipse-fitting parameters of the GFP signal displayed by the colonies.

After collection of the epithelium using forceps, the remaining matrix and TRM cells were punched using a 3-mm puncher and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube containing warm RPMI supplemented with L-glutamine (1X), 5% FBS, HEPES (1X), DNAse I (40 U ml−1), collagenase D (2 mg ml−1) and trypsin inhibitor (1 mg ml−1). Samples were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min with mechanical dissociation via vigorous pipetting every 3 min. After incubation, the sample was centrifuged at 500g for 2 min at 4 °C and washed with 1 ml of HBSS (−Ca2+ or −Mg2+; 14175095, Gibco) + 1% BSA (130-091-376, Miltenyi Biotec). This step was repeated twice. Before final cell counting, the Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was used following the manufacturer’s instructions to remove apoptotic cells and then passed through a 40-µm Flowmi filter (BAH136800040, Millipore Sigma). Afterwards, the TRM cells were transferred to a 0.5-ml tube to facilitate visualization and accurate cell counting using the Countless 3 FL before loading into the Chromium X (10X Genomics).

Nuclei isolation was performed based on 10X Genomics demonstrated protocol CG000365 rev C. In brief, single cells were centrifuged for 4 min at 400g and 4 °C. The cell pellet was resuspended in cold lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1% BSA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Tween-20, 0.1% Nonidet P40 substitute, 0.01% digitonin and 1 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor). After 6 min on ice, cold wash buffer was added (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1% BSA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Tween-20 and 1 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor) and nuclei were spun for 5 min at 500g and 4 °C. The pellet was resuspended in cold wash buffer and nuclei were counted with propidium iodide (ViaStain AO/PI, CS2-0106-5ML, Nexcelom Bioscience) using the Countess 3 FL (AMQAF2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific). After spinning, nuclei were resuspended in diluted nuclei buffer (10X Genomics) at recommended concentrations for 10X Genomics scMultiome. The quality of isolated nuclei was evaluated by microscopy with DAPI and brightfield.

According to recent reports, single-cell RNA-seq libraries were generated using 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ (v3.1) reagents according to user manual CG000315 rev E. For multiplexed scRNA-seq, single-cell suspensions of nine biological samples were individually tagged with 10X Genomics 3′ CellPlex Set A reagents according to the demonstrated protocol CG000391 rev B protocol 1. Equal amounts of tagged cells were pooled together for each sample. Three lanes of Chromium Next GEM Chip G were loaded targeting 30,000 cells per lane. Cell encapsulation and library preparation were performed according to user guide Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits (v3.1) with Feature Barcode technology for cell multiplexing CG000388 rev C. Single-nucleus multiome was performed using 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression reagents and corresponding user guide CG000338 rev F. Two lanes were loaded per sample targeting 10,000 cells per lane. All single-cell libraries (scRNA, single-nucleus RNA, Multiplex and single-nucleus ATAC) were quantified with Qubit 1X dsDNA HS (Q33231, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA Kit (5067-4626, Agilent Technologies) and were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X Plus platforms.

Sources indicate that for total single-cell total RNA-seq (VASA-seq), libraries were generated by Single Cell Discoveries, with the inclusion of a depletion step targeting the S.Tm 5S, 16S and 23S rRNAs. Libraries were sequenced aiming for a target coverage of 300,000 raw reads per cell.

We ran Cell Ranger (v8.0.0) multi-pipeline with 10X Genomics References 2024-A (hg38, GENCODE v44) as reference for read alignment, demultiplexing and gene quantification of multiplexed scRNA-seq data; Cell Ranger (v7.1.0) for scRNA-seq data of TRM cells; Cell Ranger (v9.0.1) for scRNA-seq data from FACS-sorted epithelium after infections with S.Tm WT and mutants (hereafter referred as ‘sorted infection dataset’); and Cell Ranger Arc (v2.0.1) with 10X Genomics References 2020-A (hg38, GENCODE v32) for scMultiome data. We then loaded the Cell Ranger and Cell Ranger Arc pipelines filtered count matrix to Seurat (v4.3.0.1)77 and Signac (v1.10.0)78 for further preprocessing.

Industry observers note that for the multiplexed scRNA-seq data of engineered epithelium, cells with fewer than 500 or more than 6,000 genes expressed, or total unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts exceeding 30,000, or mitochondrial gene percentage above 25% were removed. For the TRM cell data, we only retained cells with more than 500 genes, UMI counts between 1,000 and e10 and mitochondrial percentage less than 15%. For the epithelial data with and without TRM cell co-culture, we only retained cells with more than 1,000 genes, UMI counts between 3,000 and 50,000 and mitochondrial percentage less than 25%. For the sorted infection dataset, we only retained cells with more than 1,000 genes, less than 30,000 UMI and mitochondrial percentage less than 50%.

For all datasets, raw counts were normalized using the ‘NormalizeData’ function with a scale factor of 10,000. Three thousand highly variable genes (HVGs) were identified using the variance-stabilizing transformation (‘vst’) method. Data were scaled and principal component analysis was performed using these variable features. The first 20 principal components were used as input for ‘FindNeighbors’ and dimensional reduction with UMAP. The resulting graph was used for ‘FindClusters’ with the Louvain algorithm at resolution 1.0.

According to recent reports, for the multiplexed data, after inspection of regional marker gene expression, we excluded the potential foregut sample (‘don55’) marked by SOX2 and a sample with mixed ileal and colonic identity (‘IF17ile’, FABP6+ and SATB2+). We then removed ribosomal genes, mitochondrial genes, genes located on sex chromosomes and genes without proper gene symbols to avoid influence of these confounding factors to the integration of this dataset derived from multiple donors and reran the pipelines from normalization to clustering.

Epithelial cell-type annotation was initialized on cluster level based on expression of canonical intestinal cell type and regional markers, including: stem cells (LGR5, OLFM4, SMOC2 and ASCL2), absorptive cells (APOA4, FABP6 and CEACAM7), goblet cells (MUC2 and FCGBP), enteroendocrine cells (CHGA), transit-amplifying cells (MKI67), BEST4+ cells (BEST4), epithelial regional identity markers (SATB2, GATA4, CDX2 and PDX1) and leukocytes (PTPRC). Clusters with similar expression patterns were merged and resulted in a coarse-grained annotation. Differential features between proximal, distal and colonic enterocytes and colonocytes were derived from the top 500 marker genes using the ‘wilcoxauc’ function of the ‘presto’ R package on normalized RNA expression values (Wilcoxon test, logFC > log(1.1), adjusted P < 0.05). Enrichment for ‘BP’ (biological process) and ‘MF’ (molecular function) Gene Ontology was performed with the function enrichGO from the clusterProfiler package. Detected genes were used as background and all terms in the org.Hs.eg.db database were used. The enrichment score for each term was calculated by subtracting the significant −log10-transformed hypergeometric test Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected P value of the region of interest and the average of those from the other two regions. Missing values or not undefined numeric results for one region were set to the minimum of the other two regions for visualization.

Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) subtype annotation was performed following subclustering. Subtype-specific signatures (‘EC’: TPH1; ‘MX’: GHRL and MLN; ‘K’: GIP; ‘L’: PYY and GCG; ‘D’: SST; ‘I’: CCK; and ‘Prog’: NEUROG3) were calculated using the AddModuleScore function in Seurat on normalized RNA expression values. Cells were assigned to the identity with the highest score, provided the score exceeded a minimum threshold (0.1). Cells that did not meet this criteria were categorized as ‘EEC unassigned’.

In a recent development, for the multiplexed data and the sorted infection dataset, which did not resolve a cluster representing distal small intestine stem cells, we extracted stem cells from the continuum to absorptive cells based on summarized expression levels of stem cell marker genes. For the multiplexed data, we selected the top ten genes with the highest correlation with summarized scaled expression of LGR5, SMOC2 and ASCL2 across stem cells and absorptive cells and calculated the stem cell score of each cell by summing the scaled expression of selected genes. We defined cells with stem cell scores higher than the 60th percentile of positive scores as stem cells and others as absorptive cells. To reduce the noise of classification solely based on scores of individual cells, we performed high-resolution clustering (resolution = 5), and defined cells belonging to the high-resolution clusters with more stem cells than absorptive cells were defined as stem cells, regardless of their individual scores. For the sorted infection dataset, we subsetted two initial clusters (resolution = 1 from the whole dataset) with LGR5+ cells. We selected the top five genes with the highest correlation with summarized scaled expression of LGR5 and SMOC2 across stem cells and colonocytes and calculated the stem cell score of each cell by summing the scaled expression of selected genes. We defined cells with stem cell scores higher than the 90th percentile of positive scores as stem cells and others as colonocytes. The distribution of the manually extracted stem cells fits the visual inspection on the LGR5 feature plot. For the colonocyte-subtype annotation in the sorted infection dataset, colonocyte clusters with more than 80% cells from the GFP+ samples were collectively defined as ‘enriched in GFP+’, the colonocyte cluster with less than 0.1% cells from the non-infected sample were defined as ‘depleted in non-infected’, and other colonocyte clusters were defined as ‘shared’.

In a recent development, to resolve the goblet cell heterogeneity in the multiplexed data, we subsetted goblet cells from the entire dataset based on their coarse-grained cell-type annotation. The subset was re-normalized, and variable features were recalculated and reclustered (resolution = 1). We excluded clusters with enriched expression of MKI67 to get non-proliferative goblet cells and performed subclustering. We identified cluster markers using the wilcoxauc function implemented by the presto package and defined significant cluster markers with Wilcoxon rank-sum test Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05, expressed cell percentage difference (pct_in) > 10%, expression logFC > 0.1.

According to recent reports, TRM cell-type annotation was performed on the cluster level. We first annotated epithelial cells (EPCAM+), B cells (CD79B+) and proliferative CD4+ T cells (MKI67+), then annotated non-proliferative T cell subtypes based on mapping to a public adult human intestine tissue immune cell reference with two complementary approaches. We identified cell-type markers of the in vitro and tissue data separately using the wilcoxauc function with cut-off Wilcoxon rank-sum test Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05, expressed cell percentage difference > 10%, expression logFC > 0.1. We quantified the marker gene overlap significance between in vitro and tissue cell types using −log10-transformed Fisher’s two-sided exact test nominal P value. For each in vitro cell type, we got the top three tissue cell types with the strongest overlap, or the subset of top three if the significance difference between pairs of top three was larger than 10. In parallel, we calculated Spearman correlation between our in vitro and tissue cell types based on the markers defined in both systems. For each in vitro cell type, we got the top three tissue cell types showing the highest transcription program similarity, or the subset of top three if the significance difference between pairs of top three was larger than 0.1. We then annotated the in vitro T cells as the overlap of overlap-based and similarity-based matched tissue cell types. On the basis of further inspection of individual canonical marker gene expression, we manually renamed activated CD4 T, activated CD8 T and MAIT-like CD4 as CD4 TRM, CD8 TRM and CD4 TRMTH17, respectively.

According to recent reports, to construct an adult human intestine tissue transcriptome reference, we collected the count matrix and cell-type annotation of epithelial cells from three public adult intestine multi-region scRNA-seq datasets79,80,81. All datasets were processed using Seurat (v4). After merging the datasets, we performed LogNormalize normalization with a scale factor of 10,000. We identified HVGs independently for each dataset using the vst method, selecting 3,000 HVGs per dataset. We then selected integration features across datasets using the SelectIntegrationFeatures function. We ran principal component analysis using the selected integration features and retrieved the top 50 principal components. We integrated the data with Cluster Similarity Spectrum (CSS)82 stratified by sample, and default setting for other parameters. We performed dimension reduction with UMAP, and Louvain clustering based on CSS embeddings using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions at a resolution of 1.0. We compared the data without batch effect correction, integration with Harmony or with CSS integration, and chose CSS-integrated results based on visual inspection of canonical cell-type marker gene expression.

Sources indicate that to establish a consistent cell-type annotation scheme across datasets, we created a mapping between original annotations and standardized categories. We classified cells into major epithelial lineages: absorptive cells (enterocytes and colonocytes), goblet cells, BEST4+ cells, EECs, follicle-associated epithelium, stem cells, M cells, Paneth cells, secretory progenitors and tuft cells. We further refined these annotations by incorporating regional information. We defined the G2M-phased cells defined by the CellCycleScoring function in Seurat within the clusters with enriched expression of MKI67 as the transit-amplifying cells. Cell-type identities were validated using established marker genes. For rare cell populations (for example, Paneth cells and tuft cells), we calculated expression-based scores using canonical markers (DEFA5 and DEFA6 for Paneth cells; RGS13, AVIL and ALOX5 for tuft cells) and assigned cells based on these scores. To be more specific, we identified the top five positively correlated genes with summarized DEFA5 and DEFA6 scaled expression profiles across epithelium among the 3,000 HVGs as feature genes of Paneth cells. We summed up the scaled expression levels of the selected top five Paneth-associated genes for each cell as the Paneth cell feature score, and defined cells with scores exceeding 97.5th percentile of all positive scores as Paneth cells. We applied a similar procedure to identify tuft cells, with 10 tuft cell feature genes and using 95 percentile as the selection cut-off.

To establish a tissue reference for colonocyte subtype annotation in the Salmonella dataset, we subsetted to non-small intestine transit-amplifying cells, stem cells and colonocytes, integrated the data with CSS and performed subclustering based on the CSS embeddings at resolution = 0.4. We identified cluster markers using the wilcoxauc function in the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1. We selected the top 100 markers ranked by logFC from each cluster and unified them as features for comparison between in vitro and tissue colonic stem cells and colonocytes.

It has been revealed that to further reconstruct the differentiation trajectory from stem cells to colonocytes in primary tissues (excluding transit-amplifying cells), we computed a diffusion map using the DiffusionMap function in the destiny package on the CSS space and we defined the rank of the first diffusion component (DC1) as the inferred differentiation pseudotime. We ordered the cells along the pseudotime, partitioned them into 25 bins and calculated the average gene expression of each bin. We calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients between the bin average expression levels and the bin order for each gene. The 50 genes with the strongest positive correlations were selected as pseudotime-positive correlating genes, which show higher expression levels in mature colonocytes, and the 50 genes with the strongest negative correlations as pseudotime-negative correlating genes, which show higher expression levels in stem cells and early colonocytes. We then applied these tissue-derived differentiation-related genes on the sorted infection dataset. We used the AddModuleScore function in Seurat based on normalized RNA expression values of the pseudotime positively and negatively correlating genes separately. A composite differentiation score of the cells in the chip was defined as the difference between the positive and negative module scores. We ordered the colonocytes according to the differentiation score from premature to mature, partitioned them into 25 bins and calculated the average gene expression of each bin. The obtained bin average gene expression profiles are defined as expression profiles along the reconstructed pre-mature-to-mature colonocyte differentiation trajectory.

It has been revealed that to create a unified peak list across samples, we called open chromatin-accessible regions in each sample using MACS2 (v2.2.9.1) with the CallPeaks function and then quantified them with FeatureMatrix in Signac. We only kept regions located on standard chromosomes. We annotated peaks to most nearby genes using the annotatePeak function in ChIPseeker based on the Ensemble (v98) annotation. We only retained cells with ATAC UMI count between 200 and 50,000, RNA UMI count less than 20,000, RNA gene number between 500 and 5,000, mitochondrial percentage less than 50%, nucleosome signal (calculated by NucleosomeSignal) less than 1, transcription start site enrichment score (calculated by TSSEnrichment) less than 1 and hg38 genome blacklist ratio less than 0.5%. We ran the same pipeline of scRNA-seq data from read count normalization to dimension reduction and clustering as described in the previous section (‘Preprocessing and cell-type annotation of scRNA-seq data’). For the scATAC-seq data, we performed term frequency-inverse document frequency normalization on read counts using the RunTFIDF function. We defined the regions with over 1% detection rate as top features and RunSVD based on the top features. We projected cells into two-dimension UMAP embeddings and FindNeighbors based on top 2–50 latent semantic indexing.

Industry observers note that we performed major epithelial cell-type annotation on RNA cluster level based on canonical cell-type marker expression. We subsetted to colonic stem cell and colonocyte clusters, calculated the Spearman correlation coefficients between in vitro and tissue stem cell to colonocyte clusters using the in vitro-expressed colonic stem cell and colonocyte feature genes defined in the tissue reference. We performed hierarchical clustering on the in vitro clusters based on the similarity profiles and classified them into stem cells and four colonocyte subtypes indicating differential maturity accordingly. Colonocyte clusters with mostly exclusive presence in the Salmonella-infected sample were defined as infection-specific colonocyte clusters. We transferred RNA-level cell-type annotations to ATAC data, and merged subtypes that could not be clearly resolved by ATAC data as annotations on the ATAC level.

According to recent reports, we performed differential analysis for co-clustered S.Tm infection and control cells in each cluster of stem cells, colonocytes and goblet cells, which have sufficient cell numbers for robust estimation. For infection-specific clusters, which have less than 20 control cells in the clusters, we first identified matched control sample cells for each infected sample cell using get.knnx of the FNN package with k = 1 in the top 20 principal component space. We identified DEGs between matched control and infected cells using the wilcoxauc function by the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1. We applied the same procedure to identify DEGs in the epithelium induced by TRM cell co-culture except that we did not need to use the k-nearest neighbour search approach to get matched control cells as there was no condition-specific cluster.

To identify DARs between Salmonella-infected and control conditions, we implemented a statistical framework based on linear regression modelling of binarized chromatin accessibility data, with sequencing depth (UMI counts) as covariate. Specifically, for each open chromatin region i, we fitted:.

Null model: glm(e ~ UMIcounts, family = binomial).

Full model: glm(e ~ UMIcounts + condition, family = binomial).

where e represents the binarized accessibility state vector for region i across all cells. We applied a Chi-squared test comparing the two models using ANOVA. Regions were considered differentially accessible if they had Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 and showed at least a 0.5% difference in the proportion of cells with the region accessible between Salmonella-infected and control conditions.

It has been revealed that we reconstructed the gene regulatory networks from the scMultiome data along the stem-cell-to-coloncyte trajectory and each of the stem cell, colonocyte and goblet cell types shared by both control and infection conditions using Pando83 separately. We used the infection-induced DEGs and 5,000 HVGs of each data as input HVGs for Pando. We constrained our candidate regulatory regions to be either conserved in mammals (defined in phastConsElements20Mammals.UCSC.hg38 provided by Pando) or overlapped with ENCODE regions (defined in SCREEN.ccRE.UCSC.hg38 provided by Pando), and showing significantly correlated profiles with HVGs as output by LinkPeaks in Signac at the default distance threshold of 500 kb. We ran find_motifs and used the Pando-provided transcription factor-binding site (TFBS) motif database compiled from JASPAR and CIS-BP as reference for Pando to identify TFBS in candidate regulatory regions. We ran the infer_grn function with a Gaussian generalized linear model (model = ‘glm’) to infer regulatory coefficients from log-normalized transcript counts and binarized peak counts summarized to SLM algorithm-defined ATAC clusters (resolution = 10). We identified transcription factor–target gene modules using the find_modules function with default settings. We combined the modules from different datasets as inferred transcription factor–target pairs.

Recent findings suggest that for visualization, we selected the condition-dependent DEGs with the top 500 absolute value of expression log-transformed fold change between conditions and the union set of the top three-correlated Pando-predicted transcription factors of each selected DEGs. We calculated pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients of expression profiles across cell types and conditions between selected genes, reduced the dimension of obtained correlation matrix to 20 principal components using prcomp_irlba in the irlba package and further projected genes to two-dimension embeddings using umap in the uwot package with the obtained principal components as input.

We ran the AddMotifs function in Signac to add the TFBS motifs information on our detected open chromatin regions and obtained a motif occurrence matrix. To identify TFBS motifs over-represented in open chromatin regions with increased accessibility upon infection in each cell type, we ran FindMotifs in Signac on the top 200 upregulated accessible regions, with 30,000 open chromatin regions with matched overall GC content retrieved by the MatchRegionStats function as background.

We defined three comparisons to characterize the luminal effects: (1) ΔSPI-1/2 non-invaded (ΔSPI-1/2Out, GFP−) versus non-infected, (2) WT non-invaded (WTOut, GFP−) versus non-infected, and (3) WTOut versus ΔSPI-1/2Out; and three for intracellular effects: (1) WT invaded (WTIn, GFP+) versus WTOut, (2) ΔsteE invaded (ΔsteEIn, GFP+) versus WTIn, and (3) ΔSPI-2In versus WTIn. We subsetted to colonocytes. Genes detected in at least 50 colonocytes were retained, excluding features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ‘ENSG’. Pairwise comparisons were conducted between predefined experimental conditions within each colonocyte cluster. Comparisons were performed only when at least 20 cells were available in at least one condition. When one of the conditions contained fewer than 20 cells, we supplemented with cells from other clusters of the same condition that were defined as nearest neighbours of the other condition, using get.knnx of the FNN package with k = 1 based on Euclidean distance in the top 20 principal component space. Differential expression testing was performed using the wilcoxauc function of the presto R package on normalized RNA expression values. We identified DEGs between conditions per cluster using the wilcoxauc function by the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1.

We then pooled genes defined as significant DEGs in at least one comparison in at least one cluster as the union set of condition DEGs. We then calculated the colonocyte average expression levels of each condition. We calculated the expression difference between WTOut and non-infected—namely, diff_WT_vs_NI, where positive values indicate upregulation in WTOut versus non-infected—and between WTIn and WTOut—namely, diff_WT_GFP_vs_WT, where positive values indicate upregulation in WTIn versus WTOut. We ranked the gene according to diff_WT_vs_NI, took the top 50 genes as feature genes and used the AddModuleScore function to calculate the luminal effect gene module score, and applied the same procedure for diff_WT_GFP_vs_WT values for intracellular effect gene module score.

It has been revealed that we used CellChat (v2)84 to infer intracellular communications between co-cultured intestinal epithelial cells and TRM cells. Normalized expression data were extracted from the epithelium and TRM cell combined Seurat RNA assay, and cell-type labels were used to group cells for interaction analysis. We used the built-in human CellChatDB database as reference for ligand–receptor interactions. To reduce computational cost, we subsetted the expression data to include only signalling genes present in the database. Overexpressed genes and interactions were identified using the identifyOverExpressedGenes and identifyOverExpressedInteractions functions. Communication probabilities were computed using the computeCommunProb function with type = truncatedMean and trim = 0.05. We subsetted to interactions between proximal small intestinal enterocytes and immune cell types, excluding proliferating CD4+ T cells for visualization.

In a recent development, read alignment, gene expression quantification and cell filtering of the VASA-seq data were performed by Single Cell Discoveries. In brief, raw sequencing data were processed using Cutadapt (v4.9) to remove adapter sequences and homopolymers, followed by Ribodetector (v0.3.1) to filter out ribosomal reads. Processed reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STARsolo (v2.7.11b), with the parameter–soloFeatures set to GeneFull_Ex50pAS. The human reference genome used was GRCh38, ENSEMBL release 103. The S.Tm reference genome was downloaded from EnsemblBacteria Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium str. 14028S str. LT2 14028S (GCA_000022165) release 62. The resulting single-cell-level gene count matrices were used as inputs for downstream analysis in R.

Recent findings suggest that to improve the gene annotation for the S.Tm genome, we performed sequence alignment for the genes in the S.Tm strain 14028S annotation against the S.Tm strain 14028 annotation (GCF_028596185.1_ASM2859618v1). Out of the 1,542 genes with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 242 were mapped to annotated genes with common names in the S.Tm 14028 annotation by blastn85,86 with more than 90% of sequence similarity.

Industry observers note that cells without GFP signal, UMI count of less than 3,500 or External RNA Controls Consortium (ERCC) counts of less than 450 were excluded. Raw counts were normalized using the NormalizeData function in Seurat with a scale factor of 10,000.

According to FACS index sorting values, cells with GFP < 500 were defined as GFP−, 500 or more and less than 2,000 as GFPlo, 2,000 or more and 10,000 or less as GFPint, and more than 10,000 as GFPhi. For human genes, only genes detected in at least 10% of cells in at least one GFP signal group were included in the differentially expressed test. For each retained gene, expression was modelled using two nested linear models. The reduced model included log-transformed total UMI counts per cell and the percentage of mitochondrial reads as technical covariates, whereas the full model additionally included the GFP signal group as a factor. The contribution of the GFP signal group was assessed by ANOVA comparing the full and reduced models. Genes with Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. To assign directionality, we calculated the difference in average expression between the GFPhi and GFPlo groups and assigned the directionality accordingly.

For S.Tm, we applied the same differentially expressed test strategy, but only included GFP+ cells for comparison. Given the sparsity of the bacteria transcripts, we reduced the detection rate cut-off to 1%. After further excluding ERCC transcripts and features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 3,137 genes were left as input for the differentially expressed test. We used nominal P < 0.05 as the cut-off to get marginally significant bacterial DEG.

Fragment files of scMultiome are available at Mendeley Data (https://doi.org/10.17632/8pt6w6fc7m). The raw mass spectrometry proteomic files and corresponding metadata tables and scripts used are available in the MassIVE repository (UCSD) under the accession code MSV000102372. The raw flow cytometry data files used to generate the immune UMAP have been deposited in the Zenodo repository87 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21786694). Source data underlying all graphical representations used in the figures are provided as Supplementary Information. Public adult intestine multi-region scRNA-seq datasets were retrieved from an interactive website of the Space-Time Gut Cell Atlas (https://www.gutcellatlas.org/)79, ArrayExpress (E-MTAB-10187)81 and Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE185224)80.

The core scripts of single-cell data analysis are available on GitHub (https://github.com/devsystemslab/Host-microbe_interaction_model/).

R.L.-S., M.F.H., Q.Y., M.N., N.G. and J.G.C. conceived the study. R.L.-S., M.F.H., Q.Y., N.G. and J.G.C. wrote the manuscript. M.N. designed and fabricated the fluidic device and crypt stamps, with support from J.A. and S.M. M.P.L. contributed to the development of the fluidic device holding the tissues. M.N. and R.L.-S. generated the artwork design. M.F.H. and R.L.-S. designed and performed most of the experiments in the article. R.L.-S., M.F.H., M.N., N.A. and J.B. optimized the epithelium growth conditions. M.F.H. isolated the organoid lines and TRM cells from primary tissue. R.L.-S., M.F.H., M.A.-B., L.G.-T. and S.S. performed scRNA-seq, scMultiome and VASA-seq experiments. M.A.-B. and L.G.-T. generated the sequencing libraries. Q.Y. performed the computational analysis of scRNA-seq and scMultiome data, with support and data interpretation from R.L.-S., S.S. and M.F.H. M.F.H., R.L.-S. and J.A. co-developed the histomold. I.C. and S.T. performed the FFPE processing, sectioning, H&E and AlcianBlue–PAS stainings, with support from M.F.H. M.F.H. performed the immunohistochemistry and mIF stainings, imaging and analysis with support from R.L.-S. and M.N. M.F.H., R.L.-S., M.N. and L.K. performed whole-mount stainings and imaging. M.F.H., K.K. and S.K. performed the flow cytometry experiments and analysis of immune cells. R.L.-S., D.C. and I.C.-A. performed the flow cytometry and image stream experiments and analysis of epithelial cells. L.K., A.M.F. and M.F.H. performed the cytokine measurements. N.A., S.R.V., Y.B. and J.B. generated the organoid reporter lines. J.F., A.A. and C.S. performed and processed the proteomic measurements. Live imaging was performed by M.F.H., R.L.-S. and M.N., and analysed by M.B. M.H. and D.B. generated and provided the S.Tm strains. T.R. and F.G. supported with data interpretation. All authors read and approved the manuscript.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Matt Law | 19 Nov 2026 11:55, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 11:59.
  • Real Madrid will aim to post a ninth straight win in all competitions when they resume their La Liga campaign at home to Celta Vigo on Saturday night.
  • Jose Mourinho's side have serious momentum heading towards a period which will see them play eight times before the winter break in Spain halts the season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 19 Nov 2026 11:55, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 11:59.

Real Madrid will aim to post a ninth straight win in all competitions when they resume their La Liga campaign at home to Celta Vigo on Saturday night.

Jose Mourinho's side have serious momentum heading towards a period which will see them play eight times before the winter break in Spain halts the season.

There were serious questions asked of Real Madrid following their defeat to Atletico Madrid before the September/October international break, but the response from Mourinho's side to the loss in the Madrid derby has been seriously impressive.

Indeed, Los Blancos have won each of their last eight games in all competitions, including their last five in the league, which has allowed them to sit firmly in the title hunt.

Real Madrid have a record of 10 wins and two draws from their 12 league matches this season, with 30 points leaving them second in the La Liga table, only three points behind the leaders Barcelona, who had been threatening to run away with it earlier this season.

Los Blancos actually have the joint-best defensive record in La Liga this season with only 10 conceded - the same as both Celta and Atletico Madrid.

Real Madrid will have revenge on their minds in this weekend's contest, having suffered a stunning 2-0 defeat to Celta in the corresponding match at Bernabeu last term.

The victory for Celta at Bernabeu last season proved to be their first win over Real Madrid since January 2017, while it was their first league success against Los Blancos since May 2014, with this fixture dominated by the capital giants throughout history.

Celta have been solid defensively this season but have found it incredibly difficult down the other end of the field, netting only 10 times in 12 league matches, which is among the worst attacking records in the division at this stage of proceedings.

That noted, Claudio Giraldez's side did manage to put five unanswered goals past Salamanca in the first round of the Copa del Rey on November 13.

Celta's last league match ended in a goalless draw with Levante on November 8, and they currently sit 11th in the table, boasting a record of two wins, seven draws and three defeats.

The Sky Blues are also playing in the Europa League this season, currently sitting 27th in the overall table, picking up three points from their first four games of the campaign.

Real Madrid form (all competitions):.

Celta Vigo form (all competitions):.

Real Madrid have been boosted by the news that Aurelien Tchouameni and Bernardo Silva are both back in training ahead of this match.

Tchouameni pulled out of the latest France squad with a groin matter, while Bernardo left Portugal duty early due to an injury problem - both are seen as fit for this match at this stage, although it is unlikely that either will be in the starting side.

The returning Vinicius Junior - back from a domestic suspension - is set to feature down the left, with Yan Diomande, Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe potentially also all starting.

However, Rodrygo (knee), Raul Asencio (leg) and Ferland Mendy (hip) are still unavailable for the capital giants.

As for Celta, all of Ilaix Moriba (knee), Manuel Sanchez (hamstring), Alvaro Nunez (groin), Borja Iglesias (calf), Carl Starfelt (hamstring), Miguel Roman (knee) and Jones El-Abdellaoui (knee) are regarded as doubts at this stage of proceedings.

Ferran Jutgla scored twice against Salamanca in the Copa del Rey last time out, but it is expected that Pablo Duran will be given the nod down the middle.

There is also likely to be a position in the side for the experienced Iago Aspas, who has scored five career goals against Real Madrid.

Real Madrid possible starting lineup:.

Courtois; Dumfries, Konate, Huijsen, Cucurella; Valverde, Guler; Diomande, Bellingham, Vinicius; Mbappe.

Celta Vigo possible starting lineup:.

Radu; Rodriguez, Caceres, Alonso; Rueda, Antanon, Burcio, Carreira; Aspas, Duran, Swedberg.

Celta are capable of making this a tricky match for Real Madrid, but we are expecting Mourinho's side to pick up another valuable three points on Saturday.

  • Industry observers note that as reported by French news outlet ICI Alsace, Matos said: “It was a difficult decision to leave Swansea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that swansea City confirmed on Wednesday that head coach Vitor Matos had left the club to take charge of Strasbourg, with the Portuguese manager’s appointment officially announced. The Swans received compensation of around £5m, with Leon Britton and Kris O’Leary taking charge on an interim basis, alongside former defender Ashley Williams.

Matos’ departure came as a shock and it has left sour feelings from Swansea City fans. Speaking ahead of his first game as Strasbourg boss, Matos has revealed his feelings towards his former side, and what he expects from the Swansea fans.

Industry observers note that as reported by French news outlet ICI Alsace, Matos said: “It was a difficult decision to leave Swansea. I expect nothing from the fans but anger, and I understand it“.

It has been revealed that he added:“It’s a really exciting project and I felt I could help move the team forward. It wasn’t an easy decision to leave Swansea, given the emotional dimension and emotional bonds I had forged there.”.

Sources indicate that it does not seem a replacement for Matos is close with Britton, O’Leary and Williams in charge for the clash against West Brom. Rob Edwards and Tommy Elphick are reportedly on the clubs radar as potentially replacements.

Industry observers note that swansea City will be frustrated to lose another manager just as they appeared to be building towards something special. The situation is reminiscent of Russell Martin’s departure, when he was poached by Southampton.

Recent findings suggest that the Swans made significant progress under Matos, so finding a successor who can maintain a similar tactical approach should be a priority. Doing so would allow them to get the best out of the existing squad while limiting the disruption and adjustment period that inevitably comes with an unexpected change in the dugout.

Swansea City will be carefully weighing up a number of candidates, but there will be an urgency to appoint Matos’ replacement as quickly and efficiently as possible. The longer the vacancy remains, the greater the risk of disrupting the momentum they had begun to build.

Recent findings suggest that swansea City took a bold gamble when appointing Matos last season. He arrived with very little experience as a head coach, but the decision has proved to be an inspired one and could earn the club a substantial compensation fee at the very least.

Recent findings suggest that with his departure looking increasingly likely amid his interest in the Strasbourg job, the Swans should have plenty of confidence in their ability to find a suitable replacement. The Matos appointment itself is evidence of their judgement, while their recent transfer windows have also been particularly impressive.

Overall, Swansea’s recruitment of both players and staff has been very strong and has helped transform them into a much more competitive side. There is little reason to doubt that their next managerial appointment could be another success.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 19 Nov 2026 11:56, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 20:39.

Lincoln City play host to Wrexham on Saturday afternoon with just three points separating the teams in the Championship table.

While Lincoln are in 21st position in the standings, Wrexham's recent upturn in form has moved them into 15th spot.

If Lincoln managers Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw had been offered the chance to sit five points clear of the relegation zone at this stage of the season, they would have taken it.

However, three successive defeats before the November international break have left the pair with much to ponder.

Although losing 3-1 at home to Birmingham City was not necessarily a surprise, Lincoln then succumbed to a 1-0 defeat to struggling Watford.

The Imps then conceded an 80th-minute goal to lose 2-1 at Queens Park Rangers in their most recent fixture.

Sources indicate that cohen's and Shaw's priority will be to improve Lincoln's home form. Despite a 4-1 victory over Burnley on October 24, that remains their only win at the ProAmpac Stadium in this season's Championship.

As far as Wrexham are concerned, Phil Parkinson found himself fighting for his job prior to the international break.

Nevertheless, four points from home fixtures against Middlesbrough and Wolverhampton Wanderers have at least bought the long-serving boss some time.

While Wrexham remain six points behind the playoff spots, there is at least a feeling of optimism on the back of encouraging results versus the second and fourth-placed teams in the division.

That remarked, the Welsh outfit have gone five matches without recording a win on their travels, while they have netted just five times across seven away fixtures.

Lincoln City Championship form:.

Either Ivan Varfolomeev or Tom Bayliss are expected to replace Lincoln midfielder Conor McGrandles, who is serving a one-match ban.

While Ben House is available again after suspension, the attacker may only be named on the substitutes' bench.

Rob Street could come back into the team to replace Mikkel Ladefoged, depending on whether Cohen and Shaw go with a 4-2-3-1 or 4-4-2 formation.

If Kieffer Moore is ruled out of this fixture through injury, Bailey Cadamarteri may be handed a rare start in attack.

With Issa Kabore also a fitness doubt, Danny Imray is on standby to deputise at right wing-back.

Josh Windass and Nathan Broadhead are again expected to miss out through injury, while Sam Smith is a long-term absentee.

Lincoln City possible starting lineup:.

Wickens; Oyegoke, Elerewe, Bradley, Reach; Hackett, Konak, Varfolomeev, Jefferies; Draper, Ladefoged.

Wrexham possible starting lineup:.

Patterson; Worrall, Cleworth, Doyle; Kabore, Dobson, Rathbone, Whiteman, Ekomie; O'Brien; Cadamarteri.

According to recent reports, for different reasons, this has the potential to be an crucial fixture in the context of their respective seasons. Although home advantage and a two-week break could benefit Lincoln, Wrexham may edge this contest, with Parkinson likely tempted to push for all three points in a tight game.

Tech Report: Team news: 5 players set to miss Stoke City vs Birmingham City

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Championship is back after yet another international break, and we've now got a straight sprint until the Easter weekend with no interruptions.
  • The second-tier returns with a bang, as two of the sides sitting on 29 points atop the table go head-to-head at the bet365 Stadium on Saturday.
  • Stoke City, who have exceeded early-season expectations once more, will be keen not to fade away over the coming months like they did last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Championship is back after yet another international break, and we've now got a straight sprint until the Easter weekend with no interruptions.

The second-tier returns with a bang, as two of the sides sitting on 29 points atop the table go head-to-head at the bet365 Stadium on Saturday.

Stoke City, who have exceeded early-season expectations once more, will be keen not to fade away over the coming months like they did last year. A win at home against the current table-toppers, Birmingham City, would go a long way towards doing that.

Sources indicate that the Blues were ruthless over the seven-game block between international breaks, winning six of seven, and three of those wins came by at least a three-goal margin. Their form away from St Andrew's is as massive a contributor to their place atop the table, winning just one game fewer already this year than they did in the entirety of last season.

Industry observers note that but only Swansea City and Middlesbrough — two fellow quick-starters — have come away from Stoke with all three points, and Kim Hellberg's side needed a late winner to do so. This won't be an easy matchup for either, and three points will give a massive boost to both sides' promotion hopes.

These five players, however, won't be able to feature.

French attacker Lamine Cisse had started six straight for Stoke before he went down inside 20 minutes against Bristol City last month and was forced off.

The extended run in the team, plus a goal in the win at Bolton Wanderers, gave hope that the £2m arrival last summer from Bastia was starting to find his feet in Mark Robins' side, so this setback is especially frustrating.

The ankle injury he picked up should see him out until Christmas.

Ato Ampah has had a terrible time with injuries ever since he arrived at Stoke from Chelsea's academy back in January.

He's yet to make his debut for the Potters due to a series of setbacks. Last season, it was an elongated recovery from a toe injury which kept him on the sidelines, and over pre-season he suffered a setback to that recovery.

While spending time with the Under-21s, though, the 20-year-old picked up an impact injury to his knee, which required surgery and will keep him out for the foreseeable future.

It has been revealed that it's still unconfirmed whether Eric Bocat will be able to return against Birmingham. He's missed the last four games with a knee injury, which forced him off against Derby County last month.

The hope after his diagnosis was that the left-back could make his return after the international break, but he remains a doubt, with Ben Johnson and Luca Bombino waiting in the wings to deputise in his absence.

Fellow left-back Aaron Cresswell is also a doubt for Saturday's clash with Birmingham, as he nears closer to a return to fitness from a knee injury he picked up in pre-season.

The 36-year-old remained a Stoke player over the summer, signing a one-year extension after he made 25 league appearances in his debut campaign following his departure from West Ham United.

Who do you think will come out on top between Stoke City and Birmingham City on Saturday? Let us know in the comments.

Recent findings suggest that birmingham's bill of health is relatively clear heading into the weekend. James Beadle and August Priske are both available again after missing a couple before the break, and Kristoffer Lund, who missed six weeks, is also back training.

Marc Leonard looked to be on his way out of Birmingham after heading on loan to Hearts back in January, but an Achilles injury suffered weeks before the end of the campaign saw him return to St Andrew's for treatment.

He'll remain out until the Newly introduced Year, and all eyes will be on what his role in Chris Davies' side will be after his return.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli admits his newlook team need to deliver sooner rather than later

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026.
  • Sebastien Pocognoli has conceded that he doesn’t have 18 months to demonstrate that Scotland are on the right track under him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026.

Sebastien Pocognoli has conceded that he doesn’t have 18 months to demonstrate that Scotland are on the right track under him.

Appointed Steve Clarke’s successor in the summer, the Belgian’s attempts to bring in fresh faces and a fresh style of play has produced mixed results in his opening five Nations League games.

Following Friday’s win over North Macedonia, John McGinn warned the Tartan Army that it could take as long as 18 months for everything to click into place.

But ahead of the final group match in St Gallen tomorrow evening, the manager acknowledged it’s incumbent on him to accelerate that time frame.

According to recent reports, asked if he felt he had to deliver sooner, he noted: ‘Yeah, for sure, but we’re only talking about 18 months because John said that. He could have said 15 months. I don’t know. But, for sure, it needs to be quicker.

‘In 18 months, it will be the time of the Euros and that is what he meant. We have to go there and be prepared for this in 18 months’ time.

Sebastien Pocognoli  notes his Scotland team need to show progress 'game after game'.

‘For sure, game after game, we need to see improvement.

Sources indicate that ‘Some latest faces will come back in March. So, step by step we will have more ideas and in one month’s time a lot can change also.’.

McGinn also said that the players were fully behind the manager, reiterating the point previously made by Andy Robertson and Scott McTominay.

‘I can tell you that in the time we have had together the players have been doing well in terms of replicating what I ask them to do,’ the manager stressed.

‘They know that and that’s the most important part.

It has been revealed that ‘They buy in. They like it. I think they enjoy it too. You can see when players don’t enjoy it.

‘For sure, when you win it’s more enjoyable, but it would be very bad if they weren’t enjoying it and we were also not winning games.

‘So, right now I think we are working well. We give special attention to the collective.

‘In all the camps, I am very clear about what I expect on the pitch. The players wanted this when I arrived. They wanted clarity. And I think that’s what I have tried to bring.’.

To claim second place in the group, Scotland need to defeat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t win in North Macedonia.

That outcome would ensure that Pocognoli’s men would be a pot two side in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Asked what it would take to pull off what would be a stunning win in St Gallen, the manager remarked: ‘Let’s be brave, but be intelligent.

  • Aiming to avoid back-to-back league defeats, Plymouth Argyle welcome Peterborough United to Home Park for a League One clash on Saturday afternoon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 19 Nov 2026 11:56, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 20:47.

Aiming to avoid back-to-back league defeats, Plymouth Argyle welcome Peterborough United to Home Park for a League One clash on Saturday afternoon.

The Pilgrims were dispatched at the base of title-chasing Sheffield Wednesday last weekend, whereas Posh are in the midst of an on-field crisis despite a recent managerial change.

After missing out on the League One playoffs on the final day of last season, Plymouth Argyle are desperate to crash the top-six conversation this time around; however, a recent result certainly brought supporters back down to Earth.

The Pilgrims were enjoying a four-game unbeaten run (W3 D1) across all competitions before a harrowing afternoon at Hillsborough last weekend, when goals from Billy Mitchell, Davis Keillor-Dunn and Di'Shon Bernard secured a comfortable 3-0 success for Sheffield Wednesday.

Now looking to dodge consecutive defeats, Tom Cleverley's side are presently occupying sixth position in the League One table, just six points behind pacesetters Huddersfield Town and Stockport County in first and second respectively.

The Devonshire outfit are unbeaten across their past three home matches against Reading (0-0), Alvechurch (4-0) and Swindon Town (2-1) in all competitions; however, Plymouth have actually collected more points away from Home Park this season.

The summer departure of fans' favourite Lorent Tolaj to Bristol City has increased the goalscoring burden on Canadian marksman Aribim Pepple, who has netted on five occasions in League One during 2026-27.

In April 2025, Peterborough United experienced one of the proudest days in their humble history, beating a record-breaking Birmingham City side at Wembley Stadium to earn consecutive EFL Trophy crowns.

Eighteen months on, the Posh are enduring a severe fall from grace, with club chairman Darragh MacAnthony admitting that his side are not performing anywhere near the levels expected at the moment.

The form table strongly supports MacAnthony's argument, with Peterborough losing each of their past four competitive matches without finding the net, suffering embarrassing losses to Reading (0-5) and Luton Town (0-3) since the start of November.

Winning just two of his opening nine games in charge, head coach Robbie Savage has failed to turn the tide at Weston Homes Stadium as of yet, with Saturday's visitors sitting in 22nd spot in the League One rankings.

Looking on the positive side, an unexpected victory in Devon could take Posh out of the relegation zone this weekend, with Peterborough victorious on their most recent trip to Plymouth in September 2025.

As a result, Wes Harding, Mathias Ross and Alex Hatridge are the hosts' only centre-back options for Saturday's clash.

Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool

📅 20 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails.
  • As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points.
  • Industry observers note that when Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails. Managers often envisage the worst outcome when the clock ticks down, and here, in the 93rd minute, Bournemouth had a corner.

He needn’t have worried. As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points. It was a catch, too, that put the gloss on another impeccable personal afternoon.

Industry observers note that when Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient. This dour 1-0 success, though, proves he is taking them in the right direction: he is the first Liverpool manager since Joe Fagan in 1983 to start with five unbeaten league games.

Alexander Isak might have scored the goal that leaves Bournemouth winless in the Premier League but this success owed everything to Alisson’s enduring brilliance – a comment that also applies to Virgil van Dijk – the enormous promise of Jérémy Jacquet and the grit of Ronaldo Araújo.

You go to top level football matches hoping to see something that will take your breath away and how Alisson did that in the 17th minute with a reflex save from an Evanilson backheel, the shape of his body resembling a fielder in the slips diving to prevent a boundary.

It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”.

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

In a recent development, since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”.

Don’t confuse positivity about one aspect of the team as being a guide to its collective health. There was always a chance this contest would become a cagey affair and, Evanilson’s chance aside, the opening 45 minutes were as flat as you could imagine.

Iraola again played his three £100m+ signings but Bradley Barcola is still adjusting to the physicality of English football and Florian Wirtz is still finding it difficult to impose himself on a game; patience with the German will not be infinite.

He would do worse than to look at Isak, who is now on a run of four goals in four league games and is influencing games in the manner Liverpool envisaged when they broke the British transfer record to sign him last August.

Industry observers note that isak had an unusual afternoon. His only shot in the first half almost took out some low-flying pigeons, a cross early in the second half was sliced so badly that the weekend hackers on the nearby Queens Park golf course would have felt a flood of sympathy but then he got his third opening.

In a recent development, cody Gakpo, who could have been in Manchester City blue had the cards played out differently earlier this month, wriggled down the right flank and squeezed in a cross that Isak seized upon and turned in from six yards. Liverpool never looked back.

Sources indicate that alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4.

“A striker’s job is like this,” Iraola said, who badgered Isak persistently to press Bournemouth’s defence. “He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control. He has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition’s half and have more meaningful possession. And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goals.”.

One, ultimately, was enough to see off Bournemouth, whose start to the campaign is something of a riddle. They shouldn’t be anywhere near the relegation places but that is the reality and Thursday’s historic Europa League win in Real Sociedad couldn’t mask the home crowd’s frustration.

Sources indicate that “Our attitude and effort is good,” head coach Marco Rose said. “But, at this level, small things and little details decide games.”.

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola noted: “I’m obviously happy with the result because I know this is a difficult place to come, very difficult place to get three points. And we could see it, especially in the beginning of the game. In the first 20 minutes we weren’t at the level [required] and it cost us. We finished the first half better and in the second half we played better, but that beginning of the game has surprised us, not surprised us [because] we knew where we were coming but it [was] difficult for us.”.

Industry observers note that jeremy Jacquet has made the kind of quietly authoritative start to his Liverpool career that showed why there was such excitement in February within the club when they completed his deal. So much focus on so many players but Jacquet has never been anything other 7.5/8 out of 10.

Recent findings suggest that "Let's go! One of many!" Virgil van Dijk giving Jérémy Jacquet his POTM award after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/6xWvjmrF8Y.

According to recent reports, "That's a massive moment to me to play with Virgil!" 🫡Jérémy Jacquet after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth! pic.twitter.com/UsTimGME39.

Recent findings suggest that cody Gakpo has been Liverpool’s stand-out forward this term and he was at the heart of Isak’s goal this afternoon. Speaking about the job the Dutchman is doing to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, Ashley Young mentioned on Sky Sports: “Players have to step up when you lose significant players and you get the opportunities. I think Cody Gakpo is doing that. He’s a bit fortunate [in the build-up to Liverpool’s goal] but you create your own luck. He gets the ball down the line, that’s what you want to do and he puts the ball in the box. That’s what Isak’s waiting for.”.

Andoni Iraola returns to Bournemouth this weekend knowing what to expect from players he understands so well. Sadly, I do not mean Liverpool’s.

Having built his reputation creating a hard-working, well-drilled team rich in potential, Iraola is responsible for infusing those same characteristics into the most expensively assembled squad in Liverpool history.

Recent findings suggest that his first six games demonstrate it is no quick fix. The Basque coach is the first Liverpool appointment to work with more than £700m of recent signings while being entitled to feel he has been dealt a bad hand.

Everything Iraola has stated and done so far screams that he is searching for the right blend in his starting XI while having to eradicate negative traits, with and without the ball. It was telling that the excellent performance of his youngsters against Tottenham Hotspur in midweek offered the clearest hint of Iraola’s vision than anything we have seen with all the high-priced stars on the pitch.

There is a reason the Kop stood to acclaim the energy and application of youngsters Lewis Koumas, James McConnell and Trey Nyoni – and why Iraola keeps name-checking them. Iraola is indebted to them for issuing a reminder of the non-negotiables that come with being a Liverpool footballer; regardless of price tag and reputation, leaving everything on the pitch is compulsory. It is a concern that so many of the renowned players need to hear that message.

Jurgen Klopp named Florian Wirtz in his first squad as Germany manager and has mentioned that fans must refrain from expecting “special moments” from the Liverpool playmaker as a matter of course.

Of Wirtz, he mentioned: “I think he’s the player who covered the most ground at Liverpool this season, so the willingness is absolutely there.

“We have to move away from the idea that we need to see special moments from him. He is there to help us as a team. We have to make sure that Flo feels comfortable with us.”.

Wirtz has delivered seven goals and 11 assists in his 54 Liverpool appearances.

Adam Smith, 35, played for Iraola 81 times and he admitted his former manager’s visit to the Vitality will be a sentimental affair. He noted: “It’s going to be an emotional day for everyone I think, [for] our ex-manager and some of our players that have played under him, but we’ll be up for the game for sure.”.
